article.canonical_editorial_headline: September CPI: why 0.6% and 3.7% answer different questions
article.dek: In its October 14 release on September 2026 CPI, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported monthly and annual readings with different horizons and adjustment bases.
article.display_date: Written November 2, 2026 (New York) · September CPI retrospective

epistemic_claims.text: In September 2026, all-items CPI rose 0.6% and CPI excluding food and energy rose 0.3%, both seasonally adjusted
Over the twelve months ending September, all-items CPI-U increased 3.7%; CPI-U excluding food and energy increased 2.6%. Those annual figures are not seasonally adjusted.
The difference is clear; its cause and persistence are separate questions.

Monthly and twelve-month readings in the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' October 14, 2026 release on September CPI have different horizons and adjustment bases. Comparing 0.6% with 3.7% as competing answers would confuse those distinctions.

Within the monthly pair, the all-items rise was larger than the rise excluding food and energy. That comparison establishes a difference between the measures. It does not, by itself, identify a component contribution or show whether either rate was speeding up or slowing down.

The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' September CPI release of October 14, 2026 showed a lower monthly reading excluding food and energy. Giving that narrower measure more weight is an analytical choice, not proof that the all-items increase was temporary. Giving the headline more weight does not establish persistence either.

Reading the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' October 14, 2026 release on September CPI retrospectively raises a separate question: what did contemporaneous market prices show? A claim about reception would need dated price evidence; a surprise claim would need a dated expectation. The CPI readings alone cannot supply either conclusion.

article.substack_body_markdown:
September 2026's headline CPI rose 0.6% over one month and 3.7% over twelve months, according to the [U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics release of October 14, 2026](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/cpi_10142026.htm). The monthly figure is seasonally adjusted; the annual figure is not. They describe different horizons. This retrospective puts that release alongside the earlier readings and its component breakdown.

## What the annual history shows

The dated BLS releases show different paths over the 24-month window. Headline annual inflation was 2.6% in October 2024 and 3.7% in September 2026. Core was 3.3% and 2.6%, respectively. Headline reached 4.2% in May 2026 before the September reading; the path was uneven.

Core excludes food and energy. Its lower annual reading describes that narrower basket. It does not establish how long the pressure in the full basket would last.

## The monthly pace

In the October 14 release, September's monthly headline increase was 0.6%, following 0.4% in August. Core rose 0.3% in both months. At the published precision, the latest monthly pace increased in headline CPI while core's pace held steady.

The history charts preserve each month's first reading in its dated BLS release. The monthly chart therefore follows successive release vintages, rather than today's revised seasonally adjusted history. Its breaks preserve the months without published one-month readings.

## What contributed to September's increase

BLS Table 6 supplies the component effects that the headline-core gap alone cannot identify. Energy contributed 0.377 percentage points to the all-items monthly change, core contributed 0.265 points and food contributed 0.006 points. Energy was the largest of these broad contributions, while core also added to the increase.

A component's inflation rate describes how fast prices changed within that basket. Its percentage-point effect describes how much it added to the all-items change. Keeping those measures separate makes the composition of September's increase clearer.

## What the release leaves open

The component effects explain September's composition; persistence requires evidence beyond one month's breakdown. A surprise claim requires a dated expectation, and a market-reaction claim requires contemporaneous prices. The CPI figures alone establish neither.

Analysis, not financial advice. Readers decide whether to trade.
